title: Guide Teams in a Fair and Consistent Manner in an Abattoir to Achieve Set Targets and Outputs

lessons.title: Setting and explaining targets
lessons.html:
Targets give the team direction

Every abattoir team works towards targets: the number of animals per hour or per day, yield, hygiene results, zero injuries, and limits on overtime. A team performs better when it understands its targets and believes they are fair and achievable.

Good targets are SMART

  • Specific: 60 sheep per hour on line 2, not work faster.
  • Measurable: counted by the system or a tally.
  • Achievable: possible with the people and equipment available, without breaking hygiene or safety rules.
  • Relevant: linked to what the abattoir needs.
  • Time-bound: per hour, per shift or per week.

Explaining targets

At the start-of-shift meeting, tell the team the target and why it matters, for example: We have an order for 300 lambs for a retailer by 14:00, so we need 60 per hour. Explain that food safety, welfare and safety rules still come first. A target never justifies skipping steriliser use, rough handling or removing guards.

Individual and team targets

Line work is team work: one slow station slows everyone. Use team targets for throughput and individual standards for task quality, such as no cut guts at evisceration or no hide cuts at flaying. Make sure each worker knows the standard for their station.

Tracking progress

Show progress during the shift on a board or screen: carcasses done per hour against target, contamination findings, and any downtime. When the team can see progress, it can respond early.

lessons.title: Fair and consistent treatment
lessons.html:
Why fairness matters

Workers who believe they are treated fairly are more motivated, cooperate more and are less likely to be absent or start disputes. Unfair treatment, even if it seems small, quickly damages a whole team.

Fairness in practice

  • Station allocation: rotate hard or unpleasant stations, such as the gut room or hide room, where skills allow. Do not give the easy jobs to friends.
  • Overtime: share overtime opportunities according to a clear rule and record who worked.
  • Leave and breaks: apply the same rules to everyone and follow the Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997 and company policy.
  • Training: give everyone a chance to learn new stations.
  • Recognition: notice and praise good work by all team members, not just a favoured few.

Consistency

Consistency means the same behaviour gets the same response every time, for every person. If you correct one worker for not washing hands, you must correct every worker who does the same, including senior workers and your friends. Inconsistent responses make rules seem personal rather than important.

Avoiding discrimination

Decisions about work, training, discipline and promotion must be based on performance and conduct, never on race, gender, language, religion, ethnicity, union membership or where someone comes from. Unfair discrimination is prohibited by the Employment Equity Act 55 of 1998.

Discipline

Follow the company disciplinary code and the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995. Investigate first, give the worker a chance to explain, use corrective steps for minor issues and record everything. Discipline should aim to correct behaviour, not to humiliate.

lessons.title: Coaching, motivating and reviewing performance
lessons.html:
Helping the team reach targets

Coaching on the line

When a worker struggles to keep up or makes the same mistake, coach rather than shout:

  1. Observe the task and find the specific problem, for example knife angle when opening the hide.
  2. Explain and demonstrate the correct method.
  3. Let the worker try while you watch.
  4. Give feedback: what was right, what to improve.
  5. Check again later in the shift.

Motivating the team

  • Share results at the end of the shift: We did 310 lambs with only two contamination trims. Well done.
  • Recognise individuals who help others or solve problems.
  • Listen to suggestions and act on good ones.
  • Remove obstacles: blunt knives, broken sterilisers and missing equipment frustrate workers.

When targets are missed

Find out why before blaming. Was there a breakdown? Were animals late? Was the target unrealistic for the staff available? Was a station understaffed? Discuss with the team and agree on what to change. If the cause is outside the team's control, report it to the foreman.

Reviewing performance

Hold regular short reviews with each worker. Use facts: output, quality findings, attendance, safety behaviour. Agree on one or two areas to improve and support needed, such as training. Record the review.

Key points

  • Set SMART targets and explain why they matter.
  • Targets never justify breaking hygiene, welfare or safety rules.
  • Rotate stations and share overtime fairly, and apply rules the same way to everyone.
  • Base decisions on performance and conduct, never on personal characteristics.
  • Coach by observing, demonstrating, practising and giving feedback.
